questions.q: What are the two key articles in the UN Charter that authorize the Security Council to take enforcement action under collective security?
questions.a: Article 39 (determination of threat to peace) and Article 42 (authorization of military enforcement). A wrong answer (e.g., citing Article 51 — self-defense) reveals confusion between collective security (centralized UN action) and inherent right of self-defense (decentralized state action).

questions.q: Explain why the Korean War (1950-53) is considered a unique case of successful UN collective security enforcement that has rarely been replicated.
questions.a: The USSR was boycotting the Security Council over China's seat, so no veto blocked Resolution 83/84 authorizing force. A wrong answer (e.g., "UN had its own army") reveals misunderstanding that UN has no standing force — it relies on member state contributions, and Korea worked only because great power consensus existed temporarily.

questions.q: In 1990-91, Iraq invaded Kuwait. The Security Council passed Resolution 678 authorizing "all necessary means." Apply the collective security framework: Why did this work when many later cases (e.g., Syria 2011+) failed?
questions.a: P5 consensus existed: USSR (soon Russia) cooperated with US; no vital great power interest was threatened; clear aggression (cross-border invasion) triggered Article 39. Wrong answer ("UN army defeated Iraq") shows failure to distinguish UN authorization from US-led coalition execution — collective security legitimized action but did not supply forces.

questions.q: Compare the UNPROFOR mission in Bosnia (1992-95) and UNAMIR in Rwanda (1994). Analyze how the *mandate design* (Chapter VI vs Chapter VII) and *rules of engagement* contributed to failure in both cases.
questions.a: Both operated under Chapter VI (consent-based peacekeeping) despite active genocide/war — no enforcement mandate. UNPROFOR's "safe areas" lacked Chapter VII teeth; UNAMIR's mandate forbade offensive action. Wrong answer ("UN didn't care") misses structural point: member states refused to authorize Chapter VII enforcement or provide troops for robust mandates.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The Responsibility to Protect (R2P) doctrine, adopted in 2005, has strengthened UN collective security by overriding sovereignty concerns."
questions.a: R2P is a political commitment, not a legal amendment to the Charter. It has not overridden veto power: Libya 2011 (R2P invoked, regime change followed, P5 split) vs Syria 2011+ (veto blocked action). Wrong answer ("R2P made intervention automatic") confuses normative evolution with institutional reality — Security Council authorization remains hostage to P5 politics.

questions.q: Design a reform proposal for the UN collective security system that addresses the veto paralysis problem without requiring Charter amendment (which needs P5 consent). Justify each element.
questions.a: Strong answer includes: (1) Voluntary P5 code of conduct: refrain from veto on mass atrocity resolutions (France/Mexico initiative); (2) General Assembly "Uniting for Peace" procedural upgrades — automatic emergency special session after veto; (3) Regional organization standby forces pre-authorized by SC for rapid deployment. Weak answer proposes "abolish veto" — ignores Charter Article 108 (P5 consent required for amendment).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Collective security is a system where states agree that an attack on one is an attack on all, ______ to collective action against aggression.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you see a news report: "UN Security Council fails to pass ______ on Syria due to Russian veto — civilians continue to suffer." Ask: Why does one country's veto paralyze the entire world's response?
What is Collective security? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Collective security is a system where states agree that an attack on one is an attack on all, committing to collective action against aggression.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Then trace how the UN Charter tried to fix this through Chapter VII — but gave P______ permanent members veto power.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Collective security?
questions.a: Students think "collective security" means the UN has its own standing army that fights wars.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Can evaluate specific UN collective security interventions (e.g., Korea 1950, Gulf War 1991, Rwanda 1994) by applying the criteria of legitimacy, effectiveness, and compliance with Charter principles, and can explain how great power politics (especially P5 veto) shapes outcomes.
